Catalysts have a very clear definition. Catalysts increase the **speed** of chemical reactions by lowering their activation energy but they do not change the equilibrium of a reaction. (This definition has to do with how reaction speeds are mathematically defined, so ELI15 from here) Basically, catalysts can allow chemical reaction to occur at lower temperatures at the same speed compared to an un-catalyzed reaction or to react at a faster speed at the same temperature. But they cannot change how much of will react in the end. The former property makes catalysts *extremely* important for economic chemical processes sincd higher process temperatures equal higher energy / operating expenditures.

The vast majority of industrial chemical processes are catalyzed and much work is done to make catalysts to better so less precious metals are needed or high process temperatures can be reduced. Catalysis is a very interesting field in chemistry and engineering.

Edit: forgot the most important property: Catalysts are not consumed in the catalyzed reaction even though they often take part in it.

Okay first things first. 'Reactivity' is not a term used to describe catalysts. Reactivity can refer to the general speed of a given chemical reaction. So a reactant can have high reactivity. If a catalyst is present and a big increase in speed towards the reaction product can be measured, we call that catalyst 'selective' for his tendency to promote the reaction product and 'active' for the amount it increases the speed. Keep in mind that catalysts can also increase the speed of undesired side reactions so a high selectivity is a highly desirable property. Often times, catalytic metals are very active for whole groups of chemicals so finding the right formulation is the biggest challenge. Platin is very good for extracting hydrogen from organic molecules. Ruthenium is very good for inserting hydrogen in organic molecules. Nickel is great for Benzene rings. And so forth for many, many other metals and materials.

To come back to your question: if the reaction reacts measurably faster and the metal is not consumed in but takes part in the reaction, it can be called a catalyst, yeah. Catalysts dont have to be metals. For example, a certain country uses Anthraquinone, an Napthalene derivative used in the production of chemical dyes, as a catalyst in the production of paper because anthraquinone increases the productivity of the pulp and that country doesnt have that much lumber. Metals just have lots of free electrons and several oxidation states so they can act as very flexible intermediaries.
